Research Proposal: Self-Consistency Training via Automated Factual Hard-Negative
Generation## Title
FiND — Factual Negative Distillation: Improving LLM Factual
Consistency via Self-Generated Hard Negatives

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models produce coherent but factually inconsistent outputs
— they generate statements that contradict themselves across contexts,
misattribute facts, or assert claims unsupported by their training distribution.
Existing mitigation strategies fall into two camps: (1) inference-time methods
(RAG, self-consistency, contrastive decoding) that add latency and complexity at
deployment, and (2) training-time methods (RLHF, DPO) that rely on expensive
human preference data or simple synthetic negatives that are too easy to
discriminate, leading to weak generalization.

The core gap: training-time objectives lack hard negatives that are semantically
plausible but factually incorrect, produced in a scalable, automated way.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
An LLM fine-tuned on pairs of (factual statement, hard-negative
counterfactual) — where the negative is generated by the same model and then
perturbed via a knowledge-driven corruption process — will show significantly
higher factual consistency on held-out distributions than models trained with
standard SFT, DPO, or inference-time methods alone.

The mechanism is that hard negatives force the model to learn the decision
boundary between factually consistent and inconsistent outputs, rather than
merely memorizing factual-looking surface patterns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Hard-Negative Generation PipelineFor each factual triple
(subject, relation, object) extracted from a knowledge base:

1 Prompt the model to generate a natural-language sentence expressing the
triple (e.g., "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris, France").
2 Generate hard negatives by corrupting the factual triple with four
strategies:

• Entity swap: Replace subject or object with a same-type entity ("The Eiffel
Tower is located in Berlin").
• Relation flip: Replace the relation with a semantically similar but incorrect
one ("The Eiffel Tower was built in Paris" → "The Eiffel Tower was demolished
in Paris" when relation was located_in).
• Numeric/date perturbation: Offset numerical facts by a plausible but wrong
amount ("180 feet" → "280 feet" for height).
• Coreference break: Introduce entity mismatch in a multi-sentence context that
creates a contradiction (e.g., substitute a pronoun antecedent).

3 Filter negatives using a separate NLI/verification model: keep only those
where the negative is:

• Plausible (the verification model cannot trivially reject)
• Diverse (low semantic similarity to other negatives for the same triple)

Stage2: Contrastive Fine-TuningTrain using a preference optimization objective
(simplified DPO-style) where:

• Chosen: Model's own generation of the factual sentence.
• Rejected: The hardest negative that passes the filter.

The loss encourages higher likelihood of factual trajectories and lower
likelihood of the hard-negative trajectory, using the model's own distribution
as the reference.

Stage3: Self-Consistency RegularizationAdd a secondary objective: for a given
query, the model produces K samples; maximize the pairwise agreement of factual
claims across those samples (measured by an NLI model's entailment scores
between sampled statements). This directly penalizes self-contradiction at
training time.

coverage in the model's training distribution to avoid OOD trivia.

Research Proposal: Synthesizing Failure-to-Repair Trajectories for Improving
Code LLM Reasoning## Title
Trajectory-for-Code: Self-Supervised Synthesis of
Debugging Trajectories for Robust Code Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLMs are predominantly trained on (instruction,
correct_solution) pairs, either from human sources (e.g., StarCoder data) or
synthetic pipelines (e.g., CodeAlpaca, OSS-Instruct). This outcome-only
supervision has two limitations:

1 Brittle reasoning on hard problems — When the model's first attempt is wrong,
it has no training signal for how to recover. It was never shown buggy
attempts, test failures, or the iterative debugging steps that lead to
correct code.
2 Overconfident generations — Models trained exclusively on correct outputs
lack calibrated uncertainty about when their code is likely wrong, and cannot
self-correct without an external oracle.

Gap: While self-debugging and self-refine methods exist at inference time, no
systematic study has asked whether training on synthesized debugging
trajectories (attempt → test failure → bug analysis → repair → verified fix)
improves a model's code reasoning and self-correction ability at both train and
test time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary: Fine-tuning a code LLM on self-synthesized debugging
trajectories — sequences where the model sees its own buggy attempt, test
failure signal, natural-language bug explanation, and a corrected solution —
improves pass@1 on held-out reasoning benchmarks by ≥5% over fine-tuning on the
same volume of (instruction, correct_code) synthetic data alone.

Secondary: The same training yields a measurable improvement in self-correction
(ability to improve a generation given test feedback at inference time) without
requiring an external verifier during training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Trajectory Synthesis Pipeline (fully automated, no human
labels)

Given a base code LLM (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct or CodeLlama-7B) and a
set of programming problems from a training split (e.g., APPS training set or a
subset of CodeContests):

1 Attempt: Sample $k=5$ solutions per problem from the model (temperature0.8).
2 Execute: Run each solution against the problem's test cases. Categorize as
pass or fail. Collect the failing test input, expected output, and actual
output.
3 Bug analysis prompt: For each failing solution, prompt the model: "Explain
why this code fails on the given test. Identify the specific bug." This
produces a natural-language bug description. Filter by a lightweight check —
the description must mention the relevant variable or line (heuristic).
4 Repair prompt: Prompt the model: "Given the buggy code, the test failure
details, and the bug explanation above, write a corrected version." Execute
the corrected version; keep only repairs that pass all tests.
5 Assemble trajectory: (problem → buggy_code → test_failure → bug_analysis →
corrected_code). Also include the successful (problem → correct_code) paths
as positive examples.

Yield: ~3–5× more training sequences per problem (one correct path + several
repair trajectories).

To control quality, discard trajectories where:

• The bug analysis is empty or generic (<10 tokens).
• The repair still fails any test case.
• The buggy code has a syntax error (trivial).

Stage2 — TrainingFine-tune the base model on a mixture:

-50% standard (instruction, correct_code) pairs from the same problem set-50%
trajectory data (each trajectory formatted as a multi-turn chat: user → problem,
assistant → code, user → test fails with details, assistant → bug analysis, user
→ fix it, assistant → corrected code)

Train for2 epochs. Use a replay buffer where trajectory data is sampled
proportional to the number of repair steps (more steps → higher weight). Compare
against a control fine-tuned on the same total tokens but only (instruction,
correct_code) pairs.

Stage3 — EvaluationEvaluate on held-out benchmarks (see below). Measure both
static pass@k and self-correction pass@1: allow the model one additional attempt
with test failure feedback.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Training data source:

• CodeContests (training split) ~13K problems with test cases — diverse
difficulty, multiple languages.
• Supplement with APPS (training split) ~5K problems for coverage.

Evaluation benchmarks (held-out, no test set overlap):

• HumanEval+ —164 problems with80× more test cases (EvalPlus). Measures
functional correctness.
• MBPP+ —399 problems with enriched tests.
• LiveCodeBench — recent competitive programming problems, tests recency and
generalization.
• CodeContests (test split) —165 problems.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Description |

|---|---| | pass@1 | Standard functional correctness on first sample
(temperature0.2, greedy) | | pass@5 | Any of5 samples passes (temperature0.8) |
| self-correct pass@1 | First sample + one repair round given test failure
feedback. Measures the model's ability to debug its own output. | | trajectory
efficiency | % of synthesized trajectories that produce valid repairs after one
pass (measures pipeline quality) | | calibration error | Expected Calibration
Error (ECE) on the model's confidence vs. pass rate, to test whether training on
failures produces better-calibrated models |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Base model (no fine-tuning) — e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct2.
Standard SFT — fine-tuned on (instruction, correct_code) only, matching total
tokens3. Code Alpaca / OSS-Instruct style — synthetic instruction–code pairs
from a teacher model4. Self-play w/o trajectories — generate correct code,
filter by tests, train on that (no failure data)

5 CodeRL baseline — actor-critic with test pass/fail as reward (uses RL, not
SFT on trajectories)
6 Self-Debugging (inference-only, no trajectory training) — to isolate training
benefit---

Ablations1. Remove bug-analysis step: train on (problem → buggy → repair)
without the natural-language bug explanation. Isolates the value of intermediate
reasoning.

2 Remove failure signal: train on (problem → repair) only — show the model the
correct code without showing the failure context.
3 Trajectory ratio sweep: vary the % of trajectory data in the mix
(10%,30%,50%,70%) to measure diminishing returns.
4 Model scale: replicate on1B,7B, and14B models to test whether trajectory
training helps more at smaller scales (where self-correction is hardest).
5 Oracle repair vs. model repair: replace the model's own repair step with
GPT-4's repair to measure the ceiling (is the bottleneck synthesis quality or
training itself?).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Repair data is too easy — the model generates obviously buggy code
that it easily fixes, so trajectories are trivial. | Filter trajectories by the
edit distance of the repair; keep only those with non-trivial changes (>3 tokens
different). | | Model learns to generate buggy code to get repair signal —
exploits the training setup. | Keep the50% standard SFT mix as a regularizer;
never reward buggy-only generations. | | Synthetic bug analysis is hallucinated
— the explanation sounds plausible but is wrong. | The repair step must produce
executed correct code; wrong explanations that still lead to correct repairs are
harmless, and wrong explanations that mislead the repair will be discarded. | |
No improvement on single-turn pass@1 — the benefit only shows in multi-turn
self-correction. | Acceptable if self-correction improves, but the hypothesis
requires ≥5% improvement on pass@1. If self-correction improves without pass@1,
refine the hypothesis. | | Small model can't produce valid bug explanations (<1B
parameters) leads to low-quality trajectories. | Restrict the study to ≥7B
models; use1B as an ablation but expect pipeline yield to be low. | | Metric
saturation — base model is already strong on HumanEval (85%+), leaving little
room. | Use more difficult benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests test split)
where scores are lower. HumanEval+ results are still reported but are not the
primary signal. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SummaryThis proposal tests a simple, automated, and self-supervised method for
creating rich code reasoning data: instead of only generating (problem, answer)
pairs, generate full debugging trajectories — buggy attempt, test feedback, bug
explanation, repair — and train on them. The core idea is that learning how to
recover from failure should produce more robust code reasoning than learning
only from successes. The experiment is feasible with open models, open
benchmarks, and no human annotation.

This proposal represents a synthesized research direction developed through a simulated multi-agent dialogue involving roles of a Principal Investigator, Method Designer, Skeptical Reviewer, and Experiment Engineer.

### 1. Title
**Trace-to-Truth (T3): Iterative Synthesis of Execution-Verified Debugging Trajectories for Code LLMs**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
While Large Language Models (LLMs) for code have improved significantly, they often struggle with complex algorithmic reasoning and "self-correction" during inference. Current synthetic data methods (e.g., Evol-Instruct) primarily focus on generating pairs of instructions and final "gold" solutions. This approach ignores the iterative process of programming—writing, testing, failing, and refining. Consequently, models trained on static "gold" data lack the robustness to recover from their own logical errors. There is a need for synthetic datasets that capture the *process* of reaching a correct solution through execution feedback.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Fine-tuning a Code LLM on synthetic "debugging trajectories"—which include initial incorrect attempts, compiler/test-suite feedback, and subsequent corrections—will improve the model's zero-shot Pass@k and its intrinsic ability to self-debug, compared to models trained only on successful code-completion pairs.

### 4. Method
The proposed pipeline consists of four stages:
1.  **Seed Expansion:** Use a base LLM (e.g., Llama-3-70B) to generate 50,000 diverse algorithmic problem descriptions (e.g., dynamic programming, graph theory, string manipulation) across different difficulty levels.
2.  **Stochastic Generation & Execution:** For each problem, a smaller "Generator" LLM (e.g., CodeLlama-7B) attempts to solve the problem. The code is executed in a sandboxed environment against 5-10 generated unit tests.
3.  **Trajectory Mining:** 
    *   If the code fails, the error message (Traceback, Assertion Error, or Timeout) is captured.
    *   The Generator LLM is prompted to fix the code given the error. 
    *   This continues for up to 3 iterations or until the code passes all tests.
4.  **Data Curation:** Collect the sequences that resulted in eventual success. The final training sample is formatted as: `[Instruction] -> [Attempt 1 (Wrong)] -> [Error Message] -> [Attempt 2 (Correct)]`. 
5.  **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT):** Fine-tune a base model on these multi-turn "Trace-to-Truth" trajectories, teaching the model to associate specific error types with specific logical fixes.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Synthesis Source:** Derived from a mix of competitive programming prompts (Codeforces, LeetCode) and synthetic prompts generated via the "Self-Instruct" method.
*   **Evaluation Benchmarks:** HumanEval, MBPP (Mostly Basic Python Problems), and the DS-1000 data science benchmark. 
*   **Debug-Eval:** A subset of HumanEval specifically modified to include pre-written buggy code that the model must fix.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Pass@k (k=1, 5):** Standard functional correctness.
*   **Self-Correction Rate:** The percentage of problems the model can fix in a second pass given its own initial error.
*   **Reasoning Consistency:** Measuring if the model's natural language explanation of a bug matches the actual code fix applied.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Base Models:** StarCoder2, CodeLlama, Llama-3-Base.
*   **Instruction-Tuned Baselines:** Models tuned on standard Code-Alpaca or Evol-Instruct (Magicoder) datasets.
*   **Direct-to-Gold:** A model trained on the same problems but only using the final correct version of the code, omitting the failure/trace steps.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Feedback Granularity:** Comparing training with full stack traces vs. simple "Pass/Fail" binary feedback.
*   **Trajectory Depth:** Testing the impact of 1-step corrections vs. multi-step (3+) debugging loops.
*   **Negative Sampling:** Including trajectories that *never* reached a correct solution to see if teaching the model "what not to do" provides any signal.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Model Collapse:** If the initial Generator LLM is too weak, the "correct" solutions might be inefficient or use bad practices, which the student model will then inherit.
*   **Execution Overhead:** Running arbitrary code in a sandbox at scale is computationally expensive and poses security risks (mitigated by using gVisor or Docker-based isolation).
*   **Spurious Passes:** Code might pass unit tests due to weak test cases while still being logically incorrect for the general problem (mitigated by using an LLM to generate "hard" edge-case tests).
*   **Data Contamination:** Ensuring the synthetic problems do not inadvertently leak test cases from HumanEval/MBPP.

### 1. Title
**Confidence-Gated Speculative Decoding with Dynamic Draft Lengths (CG-SDD)**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Large Language Model (LLM) inference is primarily bottlenecked by memory bandwidth during the autoregressive decoding process, where each token requires a full pass of the model's weights. Speculative decoding mitigates this by using a smaller "draft" model to predict multiple tokens that the "target" model verifies in parallel. However, standard speculative decoding uses a fixed draft length ($k$). This is suboptimal: if the draft model is uncertain, it produces incorrect tokens that are rejected, wasting verification cycles; if it is highly certain, a fixed $k$ might be too short, missing opportunities for further speedup.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Dynamically adjusting the speculative draft length based on the draft model’s cumulative confidence scores—and terminating the draft sequence early when confidence falls below a learned threshold—will increase effective throughput by reducing the overhead of failed verifications without sacrificing the target model’s output distribution.

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **CG-SDD**, modifies the speculative decoding loop:
1.  **Confidence Estimation:** For each token $t_i$ generated by the draft model $M_d$, we calculate the normalized entropy or the top-1 probability $p_i$.
2.  **Dynamic Termination:** Instead of generating a fixed $k$ tokens, the draft model continues until:
    *   The cumulative confidence (e.g., product of probabilities $\prod p_i$) falls below a threshold $\tau$.
    *   A maximum budget $k_{max}$ is reached.
3.  **Adaptive Thresholding:** The threshold $\tau$ is not static. We implement a "sliding window" controller that adjusts $\tau$ based on the acceptance rate of the previous 10 verification cycles. If the acceptance rate is high, $\tau$ decreases (allowing longer, riskier drafts); if low, $\tau$ increases (forcing shorter, safer drafts).
4.  **Verification:** The target model $M_t$ verifies the draft sequence in a single forward pass. Standard rejection sampling is used to ensure the final output is identical to the target model's standalone distribution.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **MT-Bench:** To evaluate multi-turn conversation performance.
*   **GSM8K:** To test the method on reasoning tasks where draft models typically struggle.
*   **HumanEval:** To evaluate performance on highly structured code generation.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Token Throughput:** Tokens per second (TPS).
*   **Speedup Factor:** Ratio of TPS (CG-SDD) to TPS (Vanilla Autoregressive).
*   **Acceptance Rate:** Average number of accepted tokens per verification cycle.
*   **Verification Overhead:** Time spent on target model passes that result in zero or one accepted token.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Vanilla Autoregressive Decoding:** No speculation.
*   **Standard Speculative Decoding (Leviathan et al.):** Fixed $k$ (e.g., $k=5$).
*   **Medusa:** Multiple decoding heads without a separate draft model.
*   **Lookahead Decoding:** Parallel decoding without a draft model using Jacobi iterations.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Fixed vs. Adaptive $\tau$:** Compare a static confidence threshold against the sliding window controller.
*   **Confidence Metric:** Compare Top-1 probability vs. Entropy vs. Logit-gap (difference between top 2 logits).
*   **Draft Model Size:** Test with varying draft/target ratios (e.g., Pythia-160M for Llama-7B vs. TinyLlama-1.1B for Llama-70B).

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Drafting Latency:** If the confidence calculation and threshold logic add significant per-token latency to the draft model, it may negate the gains from reduced verification cycles.
*   **Threshold Oscillation:** The adaptive controller might oscillate between being too conservative and too aggressive, leading to inconsistent throughput.
*   **Hardware Bottlenecks:** On systems with very high compute-to-memory-bandwidth ratios (e.g., small models on H100s), the overhead of managing dynamic lengths in CUDA kernels might outweigh the algorithmic benefits. Implementation will require efficient batching or padding to handle variable-length drafts in a single verification pass.

answer_a:
Research Proposal: Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Mitigating Gender Bias
in Neural Machine Translation## Title
Counterfactual Data Augmentation with
Source-Side Control for Mitigating Occupational Gender Bias in Neural Machine
Translation

Problem
Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models exhibit systematic gender bias:
they disproportionately map neutral-source occupational terms (e.g., "doctor,"
"nurse") to target-language gendered forms that align with statistical
stereotypes rather than real-world distributions. On standard benchmarks like
WinoMT, models such as mBART-50 assign "She is a doctor" the masculine
translation ~85% of the time for English→Spanish, while "nurse" is feminine ~80%
of the time. This propagates occupational stereotypes and can produce
grammatically incorrect output when the context or world knowledge contradicts
the majority pattern.

Existing debiasing approaches fall into three camps — (1) post-hoc decoding
rules, (2) fine-tuning on balanced or anti-stereotypical data, and (3)
embedding-space interventions — but each has limitations: decoding rules can
break fluency, balanced data is scarce and expensive, and embedding
interventions are often task-specific and degrade general translation quality. A
method that requires only synthetic data and a single fine-tuning step, without
specialized architectures or inference-time overhead, would be broadly
applicable across language pairs and model families.

Hypothesis
Adding counterfactually augmented training examples — where
occupational nouns are swapped across genders in the source sentence — combined
with a source-side gender control signal (a special token marking the intended
target gender) will significantly reduce occupational gender bias in NMT output
on WinoMT while preserving BLEU score on standard translation benchmarks
within0.5 points.

The intuition is twofold: (a) the counterfactual data forces the model to learn
that doctor can co-occur with feminine agreement in the target, breaking the
spurious correlation; (b) the control token lets the model disambiguate
ambiguous cases at inference without requiring a separate classifier or post-hoc
rule.

Method1. Counterfactual Data Generation Pipeline

• Start with a parallel corpus (e.g., Europarl + News Commentary for
EN→ES/DE/FR).
• Tag each sentence with occupation-bearing terms using a POS tagger +
occupation lexicon (300 occupation nouns from ONET).
• For each sentence containing an occupational reference to a specific gender
(e.g., "the female doctor"), generate a counterfactual by swapping the gender
descriptor ("the male doctor").
• Also generate sentences where occupation appears without explicit gender
(e.g., "the doctor"), paired with both a masculine and a feminine target
translation obtained by replacing gender-agreement morphology in the
reference.
• Insert a control token at the source sentence head: [GENDER:M], [GENDER:F],
or [NEUTRAL]. The neutral case is used only at inference when gender is truly
unknown.

2. Fine-Tuning

• Mix counterfactual data with original training data at a1:4 ratio (pilot
experiments will test1:1,1:4,1:9).
• Fine-tune a pretrained NMT model (mT5-small or mBART-50) for1–3 epochs with
reduced learning rate (1e-5).
• Evaluate on held-out WinoMT test sets.

3. Inference Protocol

• For sentences where the source has no gender signal, pass the sentence
through a minimal gender-identification classifier (rule-based for EN:
pronoun/coreference heuristics).
• Prepend [GENDER:M] or [GENDER:F] accordingly. When classifier is uncertain,
use [NEUTRAL], which falls back to the most frequent target form.

Dataset / Benchmark- Training corpus: Europarl v7 + News Commentary v12 (EN→ES,
EN→DE, EN→FR; ~2M sentence pairs)

• Counterfactual augmentation: ~50k synthetic sentence pairs generated from the
training corpus- Bias evaluation: WinoMT (Stanovsky et al.,2019) —3,888
pro-stereotype and anti-stereotype sentences covering60 occupations across
EN→ES/DE/FR- General quality evaluation: newstest2013, newstest2014##
Evaluation Metrics| What | Metric | How | |------|--------|-----| | Gender
bias | WinoMT accuracy | % of correct gender assignments for both pro- and
anti-stereotype sentences | | Translation quality | BLEU (sacrebleu) | On
newstest2013/2014 | | Fluency loss | chrF++ | Additional check if BLEU
degrades | | Stereo type flip | Δ between pro- and anti-stereotype accuracy |
Smaller Δ = less biased |

Primary success criterion: WinoMT accuracy on anti-stereotype examples improves
by ≥20 percentage points relative to the baseline, with BLEU drop ≤0.5.

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|----------|-------------| | Unmodified NMT | mBART-50 fine-tuned on original
data only (no augmentation, no control token) | | Decoding-only | Unmodified
model + gender-inflection post-hoc rule (e.g., adjust target morphology after
decoding) | | Balanced fine-tuning | Fine-tune on a static balanced dataset
(Equalizer, Saunders & Byrne,2020) — no control token | | Embedding debiasing |
Apply Hard Debias (Bolukbasi et al.,2016) to encoder embeddings before
fine-tuning |

Ablations1. No control token: Counterfactual data without [GENDER:M/F] token →
isolates the effect of augmentation vs. control signal.

2 Data ratio sweep:1:1,1:4,1:9 counterfactual-to-original ratio → identifies
trade-off between bias reduction and quality.
3 Occupation-only vs. all-noun augmentation: Only occupations vs. all gendered
nouns → tests whether targeting is necessary or if broader augmentation works
better.
4 Rule-based vs. learned gender classifier at inference: affects how often the
control token is correct.

Expected Failure Modes1. BLEU degradation >0.5: Counterfactual data may distort
the training distribution enough that general translation quality drops.
Mitigation: early stopping based on validation BLEU; fall back to1:9 ratio or
smaller LR.

2 Control token leakage: The model may learn to ignore the token if it's
inconsistently applied (e.g., inference-time [NEUTRAL] differs from training
distribution). Mitigation: include [NEUTRAL] in training on a random10% of
sentences.
3 Language-pair dependence: EN→ES/FR (morphologically gendered
adjectives/determiners) may show larger gains than EN→DE (three-gender system
with more complex agreement). If EN→DE gains are weak, the method may not
generalize to languages with non-binary or richer gender systems.
4 Classifier errors propagate: A bad rule-based gender identifier could prepend
the wrong control token, biasing output in the opposite direction.
Mitigation: measure classifier accuracy; if <80% on a development set, switch
to a lightweight BERT-based classifier.
5 Diminishing returns on larger models: mBART-50 (611M) or mT5-large may
already encode weaker stereotyping at scale. The method may show smaller
gains on larger models — we test on both small and large variants to bound
this.
6 Anti-stereotype improvement does not close the gap: Even with a20pp gain on
anti-stereotype examples, pro-stereotype accuracy may also shift, keeping the
gap large. Success criterion uses the anti-stereotype level rather than Δ
alone for this reason.

The following research proposal was developed through a collaborative multi-agent simulation involving roles for a Principal Investigator, Method Designer, Skeptical Reviewer, and Experiment Engineer.

### 1. Title
**Latent-Space Counterfactual Alignment (LSCA): Mitigating Occupational Gender Bias in Neural Machine Translation via Contrastive Adapter Tuning**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Machine Translation (MT) systems frequently exhibit gender bias, particularly when translating from gender-neutral languages (e.g., English, Turkish) to gendered languages (e.g., Spanish, German, French). Models often rely on stereotypical associations—such as linking "doctor" with masculine pronouns and "nurse" with feminine ones—rather than linguistic context. Current solutions like Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA) often require retraining entire models or significantly degrade translation quality (BLEU scores) due to catastrophic forgetting of the original language distribution. There is a need for a modular, lightweight approach that decouples debiasing from the core translation task.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
By injecting lightweight adapters into a frozen pre-trained NMT model and training them using a dual-objective—standard cross-entropy for translation and a contrastive loss to minimize the distance between gender-swapped counterfactual pairs in the latent space—we can reduce stereotypical bias without sacrificing overall translation fluency.

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **Latent-Space Counterfactual Alignment (LSCA)**, involves the following steps:

1.  **Architecture:** Use a frozen pre-trained Transformer (e.g., NLLB-200 or mBART-50). Insert Bottleneck Adapters after the feed-forward layers in both the encoder and decoder.
2.  **Contrastive Objective:** For a given source sentence $S$ (e.g., "The doctor finished her shift"), generate a counterfactual pair $S'$ ("The doctor finished his shift"). The encoder produces hidden states $H$ and $H'$. We apply a Contrastive Loss (Cosine Similarity or InfoNCE) to minimize the distance between $H$ and $H'$ for the tokens corresponding to the occupation and the gendered pronoun.
3.  **Joint Training:** The adapters are trained on a mixture of:
    *   **Task A (Translation):** Standard parallel corpora (e.g., Europarl) to maintain translation quality.
    *   **Task B (Alignment):** A smaller set of gender-balanced counterfactual pairs to enforce gender-neutral latent representations.
4.  **Inference:** At test time, the model uses the aligned latent space to generate translations that are more sensitive to specific context rather than prior stereotypical probabilities.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Training:** A subset of WMT23 parallel data for general translation quality, augmented with a synthetic counterfactual dataset generated using the "Gender-Neutral Pipeline" (swapping pronouns and names in English).
*   **Evaluation:** 
    *   **WinoMT:** A standard challenge set for gender bias in MT.
    *   **MuST-SHE:** A dataset for evaluating gender bias in speech-to-text/translation contexts.
    *   **FLORES-200:** To ensure no degradation in general translation performance across multiple language pairs.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Primary Bias Metric:** Gender Accuracy (Acc) and $\Delta G$ (the difference in accuracy between masculine and feminine professional terms) as defined in the WinoMT benchmark.
*   **Translation Quality:** BLEU, chrF++, and COMET scores to ensure the "utility" of the model remains intact.
*   **Bias Amplification:** Measuring the change in the ratio of masculine/feminine output relative to the input distribution.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Original Pre-trained Model:** NLLB-200 (No debiasing).
*   **CDA-Fine-tuning:** Fine-tuning the entire model on counterfactual augmented data.
*   **Post-processing:** A rule-based system that replaces pronouns in the output based on a gender-neutrality dictionary.
*   **Null-Space Projection (INLP):** A linear projection method used to remove gender information from word embeddings.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Adapter Placement:** Compare encoder-only vs. decoder-only vs. dual-adapter configurations.
*   **Loss Weighting:** Vary the weight $\lambda$ of the contrastive loss relative to the cross-entropy loss.
*   **Data Ratio:** Test performance when varying the percentage of counterfactual data (1%, 5%, 10%) in the training mix.
*   **Frozen vs. Tuned:** Compare LSCA adapters against full model fine-tuning.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Syntactic Mismatch:** In languages with heavy grammatical gender (e.g., French), changing a pronoun requires changing adjectives and articles. If the latent alignment only focuses on the pronoun, the decoder may produce grammatically inconsistent sentences (e.g., masculine noun with feminine adjective).
*   **Semantic Drift:** Excessive contrastive alignment might "blur" the latent space so much that the model loses the ability to distinguish between actual gendered contexts (e.g., "The king" vs. "The queen").
*   **Feasibility:** While adapters are efficient, generating high-quality counterfactual pairs for non-English source languages is difficult and may require LLM-based augmentation, increasing the preprocessing pipeline's complexity.

Research Proposal: Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Mitigating Gender Bias
in Neural Machine Translation## Title
Counterfactual Data Augmentation with
Source-Side Control for Mitigating Occupational Gender Bias in Neural Machine
Translation

Problem
Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models exhibit systematic gender bias:
they disproportionately map neutral-source occupational terms (e.g., "doctor,"
"nurse") to target-language gendered forms that align with statistical
stereotypes rather than real-world distributions. On standard benchmarks like
WinoMT, models such as mBART-50 assign "She is a doctor" the masculine
translation ~85% of the time for English→Spanish, while "nurse" is feminine ~80%
of the time. This propagates occupational stereotypes and can produce
grammatically incorrect output when the context or world knowledge contradicts
the majority pattern.

Existing debiasing approaches fall into three camps — (1) post-hoc decoding
rules, (2) fine-tuning on balanced or anti-stereotypical data, and (3)
embedding-space interventions — but each has limitations: decoding rules can
break fluency, balanced data is scarce and expensive, and embedding
interventions are often task-specific and degrade general translation quality. A
method that requires only synthetic data and a single fine-tuning step, without
specialized architectures or inference-time overhead, would be broadly
applicable across language pairs and model families.

Hypothesis
Adding counterfactually augmented training examples — where
occupational nouns are swapped across genders in the source sentence — combined
with a source-side gender control signal (a special token marking the intended
target gender) will significantly reduce occupational gender bias in NMT output
on WinoMT while preserving BLEU score on standard translation benchmarks
within0.5 points.

The intuition is twofold: (a) the counterfactual data forces the model to learn
that doctor can co-occur with feminine agreement in the target, breaking the
spurious correlation; (b) the control token lets the model disambiguate
ambiguous cases at inference without requiring a separate classifier or post-hoc
rule.

Method1. Counterfactual Data Generation Pipeline

• Start with a parallel corpus (e.g., Europarl + News Commentary for
EN→ES/DE/FR).
• Tag each sentence with occupation-bearing terms using a POS tagger +
occupation lexicon (300 occupation nouns from ONET).
• For each sentence containing an occupational reference to a specific gender
(e.g., "the female doctor"), generate a counterfactual by swapping the gender
descriptor ("the male doctor").
• Also generate sentences where occupation appears without explicit gender
(e.g., "the doctor"), paired with both a masculine and a feminine target
translation obtained by replacing gender-agreement morphology in the
reference.
• Insert a control token at the source sentence head: [GENDER:M], [GENDER:F],
or [NEUTRAL]. The neutral case is used only at inference when gender is truly
unknown.

2. Fine-Tuning

• Mix counterfactual data with original training data at a1:4 ratio (pilot
experiments will test1:1,1:4,1:9).
• Fine-tune a pretrained NMT model (mT5-small or mBART-50) for1–3 epochs with
reduced learning rate (1e-5).
• Evaluate on held-out WinoMT test sets.

3. Inference Protocol

• For sentences where the source has no gender signal, pass the sentence
through a minimal gender-identification classifier (rule-based for EN:
pronoun/coreference heuristics).
• Prepend [GENDER:M] or [GENDER:F] accordingly. When classifier is uncertain,
use [NEUTRAL], which falls back to the most frequent target form.

Dataset / Benchmark- Training corpus: Europarl v7 + News Commentary v12 (EN→ES,
EN→DE, EN→FR; ~2M sentence pairs)

• Counterfactual augmentation: ~50k synthetic sentence pairs generated from the
training corpus- Bias evaluation: WinoMT (Stanovsky et al.,2019) —3,888
pro-stereotype and anti-stereotype sentences covering60 occupations across
EN→ES/DE/FR- General quality evaluation: newstest2013, newstest2014##
Evaluation Metrics| What | Metric | How | |------|--------|-----| | Gender
bias | WinoMT accuracy | % of correct gender assignments for both pro- and
anti-stereotype sentences | | Translation quality | BLEU (sacrebleu) | On
newstest2013/2014 | | Fluency loss | chrF++ | Additional check if BLEU
degrades | | Stereo type flip | Δ between pro- and anti-stereotype accuracy |
Smaller Δ = less biased |

Primary success criterion: WinoMT accuracy on anti-stereotype examples improves
by ≥20 percentage points relative to the baseline, with BLEU drop ≤0.5.

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|----------|-------------| | Unmodified NMT | mBART-50 fine-tuned on original
data only (no augmentation, no control token) | | Decoding-only | Unmodified
model + gender-inflection post-hoc rule (e.g., adjust target morphology after
decoding) | | Balanced fine-tuning | Fine-tune on a static balanced dataset
(Equalizer, Saunders & Byrne,2020) — no control token | | Embedding debiasing |
Apply Hard Debias (Bolukbasi et al.,2016) to encoder embeddings before
fine-tuning |

Ablations1. No control token: Counterfactual data without [GENDER:M/F] token →
isolates the effect of augmentation vs. control signal.

2 Data ratio sweep:1:1,1:4,1:9 counterfactual-to-original ratio → identifies
trade-off between bias reduction and quality.
3 Occupation-only vs. all-noun augmentation: Only occupations vs. all gendered
nouns → tests whether targeting is necessary or if broader augmentation works
better.
4 Rule-based vs. learned gender classifier at inference: affects how often the
control token is correct.

Expected Failure Modes1. BLEU degradation >0.5: Counterfactual data may distort
the training distribution enough that general translation quality drops.
Mitigation: early stopping based on validation BLEU; fall back to1:9 ratio or
smaller LR.

inconsistently applied (e.g., inference-time [NEUTRAL] differs from training
distribution). Mitigation: include [NEUTRAL] in training on a random10% of
sentences.

adjectives/determiners) may show larger gains than EN→DE (three-gender system
with more complex agreement). If EN→DE gains are weak, the method may not
generalize to languages with non-binary or richer gender systems.

anti-stereotype examples, pro-stereotype accuracy may also shift, keeping the
gap large. Success criterion uses the anti-stereotype level rather than Δ
alone for this reason.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Knowledge Injection via Confidence-Gated Adapter
Fusion for Domain-Specific LLMs## Title
Confidence-Gated Adapter Fusion for
Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts During Domain-Specific LLM Injection

Problem
Domain-specific LLM deployment (legal, medical, finance) requires
injecting specialized knowledge into general-purpose pre-trained models. Three
interrelated challenges remain unresolved:

1 Knowledge conflicts — injected domain facts contradict or compete with the
model's pre-training knowledge, causing inconsistent behavior depending on
prompt phrasing.
2 Selective forgetting — fine-tuning on domain text degrades general-language
capabilities, especially on reasoning and rare-token recall.
3 Sub-domain interference — a single domain (e.g., clinical medicine) contains
heterogeneous sub-domains (radiology, pathology, pharmacology) that interfere
when injected via a single adapter or fine-tuning run.

Current solutions (full fine-tuning, RAG, LoRA, model editing) each address only
a subset of these. No method jointly handles all three while providing per-input
routing between base and injected knowledge.

Hypothesis
Confidence-gated routing — where the model dynamically selects between
base knowledge and injected domain knowledge based on its own predictive
uncertainty — reduces knowledge conflicts and sub-domain interference compared
to monolithic injection, while preserving general capabilities better than full
fine-tuning and matching the domain accuracy of state-of-the-art fixed injection
methods.

More concretely: an adapter mixture with a learned confidence-gating mechanism
will achieve higher domain-specific accuracy and lower general-task degradation
than the Pareto frontier of existing injection methods.

Method
Architecture. Start with a frozen base LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B). We train a
set of k lightweight LoRA adapters, each specialized on a distinct sub-domain
cluster of the target domain (clusters discovered via topic modeling or
metadata-driven splits). A small learned confidence gate is trained to produce,
for each input token/sequence: (a) a routing weight over the k adapters, and (b)
a scalar β ∈ [0,1] that mixes the adapter output with the base model's original
hidden state. When β is low, the model relies on base knowledge; when high,
injected knowledge dominates.

Gate architecture. A2-layer MLP over the hidden state of the last layer at the
final token position, outputting a softmax over adapters and a sigmoid-gated β.
Trained jointly with adapters via a regularized objective.

Training objective. Two terms:

• Domain accuracy — standard cross-entropy on domain data, but weighted by a
per-sample confidence bonus that down-weights examples the base model already
answers well (to focus injection on genuinely novel knowledge).
• General capability preservation — a distillation regularizer that penalizes
large β when the base model's output distribution on held-out general
benchmarks (MMLU subsets, GSM8K) has low entropy (high confidence),
preventing unnecessary overrides.

Inference. Single forward pass per token. Gating adds negligible latency (<1%
parameter overhead).

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct a multi-sub-domain biomedical benchmark from
public sources:

Sub-domain           Dataset                            Size         Source
Clinical guidelines  MedQA (subset)                     1.2K Q&A     USMLE
Pharmacology         DrugBank QA                        800 QA       DrugBank
Radiology reports    MIMIC-III (report impressions)     2K excerpts  PhysioNet
Molecular biology    PubMedQA                           1K QA        PubMed
General (probe)      MMLU (biomedical subset) +3        2.5K         MMLU
general sections

We also collect a training corpus by pooling the full source documents (not just
QA pairs) for each sub-domain, filtering for overlap with pre-training data to
remove ~90% intersection (document-level dedup against C4/RedPajama using
MinHash).

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Rationale |

|---|---|---| | Domain accuracy | Per sub-domain accuracy (F1/MCC for binary
tasks); macro-average | Measures injection effectiveness | | General retention |
Δ(MMLU_full), Δ(GSM8K) — absolute drop from pre-injection | Measures forgetting
| | Knowledge consistency | Counterfactual accuracy — same fact queried with3
phrasings, pass@1 agreement | Measures conflict robustness | | Sub-domain
interference | When querying sub-domain A, compute logit change on sub-domain B
adapters' outputs | Measures cross-talk | | Routing interpretability | Spearman
correlation between β and ground-truth fact novelty (was this fact in
pre-training?) | Validates gating works as intended |

Baselines1. Full fine-tuning — domain corpus,1 epoch, AdamW.

2 Prompt-based injection — zero-shot with domain-relevant system prompt (no
parameter update).
3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — ColBERTv2 retriever over domain
corpus; top-3 chunks prepended to prompt.
4 Single LoRA — one rank-32 LoRA on all domain data.
5 Mixture of Adapters (fixed routing) — same k adapters, but routing weights
hard-coded by sub-domain label (oracle routing). Upper-bound measure.
6 Knowledge-editing baseline (MEMIT) — model editing at scale on the training
corpus.

Ablations1. No confidence gating — always mix with uniform β =0.5. Isolates the
benefit of adaptive routing.

2 No sub-domain clustering — single adapter with gating. Tests whether multiple
adapters matter.
3 No regularization term — train only on domain accuracy. Measures how much
general retention comes from the distillation regularizer vs. adapter
architecture alone.
4 Varying k —                                                                  Goodbye!

This proposal represents a synthesized research direction developed through a multi-agent simulation involving a Principal Investigator, Method Designer, Skeptic, and Experiment Engineer.

### 1. Title
**Dynamic Knowledge Gating (DKG): Mitigating Knowledge Conflict and Forgetting in Domain-Specific LLM Injection**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Injecting domain-specific knowledge (e.g., medical, legal, or proprietary technical data) into Large Language Models (LLMs) via fine-tuning often results in two primary failure modes: **catastrophic forgetting** of general-purpose reasoning and **knowledge conflict**, where the model struggles to reconcile general-world facts with specialized domain nuances. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses some of these issues, it suffers from high latency and context window limitations. There is a critical need for a parameter-efficient method that allows the model to "switch" into a domain-specific state without degrading its underlying foundational capabilities.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
By implementing a learned, token-level gating mechanism that modulates the contribution of domain-specific Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) weights based on the input context, a model can achieve superior domain accuracy compared to standard fine-tuning while maintaining baseline performance on general benchmarks.

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **Dynamic Knowledge Gating (DKG)**, consists of the following components:
*   **Dual-Path Architecture:** A frozen backbone (e.g., Llama-3-8B) equipped with domain-specific LoRA adapters ($A_{dom}, B_{dom}$) in the Attention and MLP layers.
*   **Contextual Router:** A lightweight, trainable gating module (a 2-layer MLP) that takes the hidden state $h_t$ at each layer and produces a scalar weight $g_t \in [0, 1]$.
*   **Gated Forward Pass:** The output of a layer is computed as: $y = W_{frozen}x + g_t(A_{dom}B_{dom}x)$.
*   **Two-Stage Training:** 
    1.  **Warm-up:** Train the LoRA adapters on domain-specific corpora using standard Causal Language Modeling (CLM) loss.
    2.  **Gating Alignment:** Freeze the LoRA adapters and the backbone. Train the router using a balanced mix of domain data and general-purpose instruction data. The router is incentivized to minimize the loss on domain tokens by increasing $g_t$, while minimizing the divergence from the frozen model’s original output on general tokens by decreasing $g_t$.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Domain Data:** The **PubMed** (Medical) or **FreeLaw** (Legal) subsets of the Pile.
*   **General Data:** A 5% sample of the **ShareGPT** or **OpenOrca** datasets to represent general reasoning and instruction following.
*   **Evaluation Set:** **MedQA** (for medical) or **LegalBench** (for legal), combined with **MMLU** (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) to monitor general performance degradation.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Domain Accuracy:** Zero-shot and few-shot accuracy on MedQA/LegalBench.
*   **Retention Rate:** The ratio of MMLU scores post-injection vs. the original base model.
*   **Knowledge Conflict Score (KCS):** A custom metric measuring the model's ability to prioritize domain-specific answers over general-world answers when presented with ambiguous prompts (e.g., "What is the limitation of 'discovery'?" in a legal vs. general context).

### 7. Baselines
*   **Full Fine-Tuning (FFT):** Standard fine-tuning on domain data.
*   **Static LoRA:** Standard LoRA without the gating mechanism (fixed $g_t = 1$).
*   **Vanilla RAG:** The frozen base model using a vector database of the domain corpus.
*   **Rehearsal-based Fine-Tuning:** LoRA training with a static playback of general-purpose data.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Router Granularity:** Compare token-level gating vs. sentence-level gating vs. layer-level gating.
*   **Gating Input:** Compare using the hidden state $h_t$ as router input vs. using the raw input embedding.
*   **Fixed Gating:** Testing performance with a hard-coded gate (e.g., $g_t = 0.5$) to validate the necessity of the learned router.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Router Overfitting:** The router might learn to "always-on" the domain adapter if the domain data is too diverse, leading to the same forgetting seen in standard LoRA.
*   **Training Complexity:** The two-stage training process requires careful balancing of the "Gating Alignment" phase to ensure the router doesn't collapse to zero.
*   **Inference Overhead:** While the router is small, adding a gating operation to every layer and every token increases the total TFLOPS of the forward pass, potentially impacting latency compared to static LoRA.

Decomposing a complex extraction schema into atomic, single-relation sub-tasks, followed by a multi-agent verification loop that requires evidence-span grounding, will significantly reduce hallucination rates and improve F1-scores compared to monolithic, single-pass extraction.

The proposed system follows a three-stage pipeline:

1.  **Schema Decomposition:** Given a complex schema (e.g., 20 entity types, 30 relations), a "Planner" agent breaks the task into atomic extraction units. Each unit focuses on one primary entity category or a small cluster of logically related triplets.

Conversational Agents## Title
Evaluating the Evaluators: A Comparative Study of
User Experience Assessment Methods for LLM-Based Conversational Agents

User experience (UX) evaluation for LLM-based conversational agents lacks
a validated, standardized methodology. Researchers and practitioners currently
rely on ad-hoc combinations of:

• General-purpose UX questionnaires (SUS, UEQ, QUIS) designed for traditional
software- Behavioral proxies (task completion rate, response time) that may
miss novel failure modes like hallucination or sycophancy- Emerging
"LLM-as-judge" automated evaluation, which has unknown validity as a UX
proxyNo published work systematically compares these approaches on the same
set of LLM interactions, making it impossible to know which method (or
combination) best captures perceived quality, trust, and satisfaction — the
core dimensions of LLM UX.

Hypothesis1. Primary: Standardized UX questionnaires (SUS, UEQ) exhibit
moderate-to-weak correlation with task-level behavioral metrics (completion
rate, time-on-task, repair frequency) when applied to LLM interactions, because
LLM failures (plausible-sounding errors) differ qualitatively from GUI failures.

2 Secondary: An LLM-as-judge evaluator fine-tuned on human UX ratings can
approximate mean UEQ scores within ±0.5 scale points across a held-out set of
interaction scenarios, but will fail systematically on specific failure types
(hallucination, refusal, sycophancy) that require human judgment.
3 Tertiary: A composite evaluation combining behavioral metrics + a short
(3-item) custom UX scale achieves higher test-retest reliability (ICC >0.75)
than any single method alone.

Method
A controlled within-subjects experiment with three UX evaluation
conditions applied to the same set of24 prerecorded LLM interaction sessions:

Interaction Sessions (Stimuli)

24 sessions crossing:

• 2 LLMs: GPT-4o, Llama3.170B- 3 task types: factual QA, creative writing,
decision-making/planning- 4 output quality levels (validated by expert
raters): correct + fluent, correct but verbose, fluent but incorrect
(hallucination), incoherentEach session is a3–5 turn interaction shown as a
recorded transcript + final output.

Evaluation Conditions (Independent Variable)

1 Standardized questionnaires: SUS (10 items), UEQ (26 items), and a3-item
custom LLM-UX scale (satisfaction, trust, output quality) administered after
each session.
2 Behavioral metrics: Task completion (binary), time-on-task, number of user
repairs/rewrites, confidence-rated correctness (user-reported) — collected
during interaction.
3 LLM-as-judge: An LLM (same models under test + a held-out judge model)
prompted to rate each session on the same3-item LLM-UX scale, given system
prompt templates from Zheng et al. (2024).

Procedure-60 participants (power analysis: within-subjects,24 sessions, α =0.05,
β =0.80 → n ≥48 for medium effect)

• Each participant rated12 sessions via questionnaires and12 sessions via
behavioral interaction recording + self-report- LLM-as-judge evaluated all24
sessions ×3 judge model variants- Randomize session and condition order###
Analysis- R1 (questionnaire vs behavioral): Spearman correlations between
SUS/UEQ scores and behavioral metrics; Bland-Altman plots for agreement- R2
(LLM-as-judge accuracy): MAE, Pearson r, and confusion matrices between LLM
ratings and human questionnaire scores; stratified error analysis by failure
type- R3 (composite): Intraclass correlation (ICC(2,1)) for each method and
the weighted composite; bootstrap CIs## Dataset / Benchmark
No existing
benchmark fully covers this. We construct and release LLM-UX-Eval-24, a
dataset of24 curated interaction sessions with:
• Transcripts and final outputs (JSON format)
• Expert-validated failure type labels (gold standard)
• Human UX ratings from10 pilot participants (for validation prior to main
study)
• Behavioral log templates for replicationSize:24 sessions ×60 participants
=1,440 human evaluation data points;24 ×3 judge models =72 LLM-as-judge
ratings.

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | Target |

|---|---|---| | Convergent validity | Spearman ρ between methods | >0.5 for
same-construct pairs | | LLM-as-judge accuracy | MAE vs human mean | <0.5 (on1–5
scale) | | LLM-as-judge bias | Mean signed error per failure type | Report per
type | | Test-retest reliability | ICC(2,1) on20% repeated sessions | >0.70 | |
Composite reliability | ICC(2,1) of weighted composite | >0.75 | | Time cost |
Minutes per evaluation session | Report descriptive |

Baselines1. Single-method baselines: Each evaluation method (SUS, UEQ,
behavioral-only, LLM-as-judge) treated as the sole UX assessment — this is
current practice in published LLM evaluations.

2 GUI-trained UX norms: SUS and UEQ industry benchmarks (e.g., SUS mean =68)
used as-is without LLM-specific adaptation — the implicit default in most
current work.
3 Random judge: LLM-as-judge with shuffled labels as a lower-bound sanity check
for correlation significance.

Ablations1. Questionnaire length: Does UEQ (26 items) outperform the3-item
LLM-UX scale in discriminability? Remove UEQ data and re-fit models.

2 Judge model: Replace LLM judge with GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-4o — how much does
judge capability matter?
3 Prompt template: Test3 prompt variants (zero-shot, few-shot with2 examples,
expert-designed rubric) — is prompt engineering the dominant factor in
LLM-as-judge validity?
4 Task type: Remove one task type at a time — are effects driven by a specific
interaction type?

behavioral metrics may measure different latent constructs (perception vs.
performance), yielding weak ρ even if both are valid — this would invalidate the
composite approach but still be a useful finding (recommending both as separate
axes).

mean) or correlate only with surface features (output length, readability)
rather than substantive quality, rendering them useless as UX proxies. This
is the most likely failure mode based on prior LLM-as-judge critiques.
3 Carryover effects: Participants who rate via behavioral metrics first may
anchor expectations when later using questionnaires. Mitigated by
randomization and tested via period effect analysis.
4 Fatigue:12 sessions per participant may induce satisficing on later ratings.
Mitigated by capping sessions at12 (≈40 min total) and embedding attention
checks (repeated sessions with known scores).
5 Generalizability: All interactions use English text-only outputs. Findings
may not transfer to multimodal, voice, or non-English LLM interactions.
Stated explicitly as a limitation.

This proposal represents the consensus of a multi-agent virtual team (Principal Investigator, Method Designer, Skeptical Reviewer, and Experiment Engineer) focused on moving LLM evaluation from static benchmarks to interactive user-centric metrics.

### 1. Title
**The Interaction Cost Metric (ICM): Quantifying LLM User Experience through Simulated Iterative Refinement**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current Large Language Model (LLM) evaluations focus primarily on "one-shot" accuracy (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K). However, in real-world scenarios, user experience (UX) is defined by the **Interaction Cost**: the amount of effort (prompt revisions, clarifications, and manual editing) a user must expend to reach a satisfactory output. A model that is highly accurate but requires hyper-specific prompt engineering offers a poorer UX than a "steerable" model that converges on the user’s intent within one or two natural language turns. There is currently no standardized, automated metric to quantify this iterative friction.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
The "Interaction Cost"—measured by the number of tokens and semantic distance traveled across multiple prompt revisions required to reach a goal—will reveal UX disparities between models that are otherwise ranked similarly on static benchmarks. Specifically, we hypothesize that models with higher "instruction-following robustness" will exhibit lower Interaction Cost regardless of their raw knowledge parameters.

### 4. Method
The framework employs a "User-System Simulation" loop:
1.  **Goal Definition:** A set of complex tasks (e.g., "Write a Python script to scrape X but only using library Y") is defined with a hidden "Success Criterion."
2.  **The User Agent:** A separate, highly capable LLM (e.g., GPT-4o) acts as the "User." It is given the goal but is restricted to providing natural, slightly underspecified initial prompts.
3.  **The Subject LLM:** The model being evaluated.
4.  **The Interaction Loop:** 
    *   The User Agent provides a prompt.
    *   The Subject LLM responds.
    *   A "Critic Agent" evaluates if the response meets the Success Criterion.
    *   If not, the User Agent is given the response and must provide a *refinement* (e.g., "No, I meant without using the requests library").
5.  **Termination:** The loop ends upon success or after 5 failed turns.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
We propose the **Iterative-UX Benchmark (I-UXB)**, consisting of 500 tasks across four domains:
*   **Code Refactoring:** Transforming legacy code with specific constraints.
*   **Creative Constraints:** Writing prose with strict stylistic and structural requirements.
*   **Nuanced Reasoning:** Solving logic puzzles where the user gradually reveals clues.
*   **Instruction Compliance:** Following multi-step formatting instructions that are often ignored in one-shot settings.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Turns-to-Success (TTS):** The average number of iterations required to meet the critic's criteria.
*   **Refinement Semantic Distance (RSD):** The cosine distance between the initial prompt and the final successful prompt (measuring how much the user had to change their original intent to accommodate the model).
*   **Total Token Friction (TTF):** Sum of all user tokens across the interaction (a proxy for "typing effort").
*   **UX Score:** A weighted aggregate: $1 / (TTS \times \log(TTF))$.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Raw Accuracy Baseline:** Standard one-shot performance on the same tasks.
*   **Human Proxy:** A small-scale study (n=20) where human users perform the same tasks to validate if the "User Agent" behavior correlates with human frustration levels.
*   **Model Comparison:** Comparison across model families (e.g., Llama-3-70B vs. GPT-4 vs. Claude 3.5 Sonnet).

### 8. Ablations
*   **User Agent Persona:** Varying the "patience" and "expertise" of the User Agent (e.g., a "Novice User" agent that gives vague feedback vs. an "Expert User" agent that gives technical feedback).
*   **Feedback Granularity:** Testing the loop where the Critic Agent provides the User Agent with specific reasons for failure vs. the User Agent having to "guess" why the model failed.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **User Agent Bias:** The LLM acting as the "User" might be biased toward models from the same family (e.g., a GPT-based User Agent might "understand" a GPT-based Subject LLM more easily).
*   **Criterion Drift:** The "Critic Agent" might become more or less lenient over multiple turns.
*   **Computational Cost:** Running multi-turn simulations for thousands of samples is significantly more expensive than one-shot benchmarking.
*   **Feasibility Risk:** Ensuring the "Success Criterion" is objective enough for the Critic Agent to judge consistently across different model responses.

This proposal represents the consensus of a multi-agent virtual research team (Principal Investigator, Method Designer, Skeptical Reviewer, and Experiment Engineer) focused on optimizing the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff in LLM evaluation.

### 1. Title
**Information-Theoretic Item Pruning (ITIP): Constructing Minimalist, High-Fidelity LLM Leaderboards**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current LLM leaderboards (e.g., MMLU, OpenCompass) rely on thousands of static test items. This leads to high computational costs, slow iteration cycles, and significant redundancy, as many questions fail to distinguish between top-tier models or provide overlapping information. As models scale, the cost of exhaustive evaluation becomes a bottleneck for researchers. There is a critical need for a methodology that identifies the "minimal spanning set" of evaluation items that preserves the global ranking of models.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
A subset of evaluation items—selected based on high **discrimination power** (via Item Response Theory) and low **inter-item redundancy** (via Mutual Information)—can replicate the model rankings of a full-scale benchmark (e.g., 10,000+ items) using less than 20% of the original data, maintaining a Spearman rank correlation of $\rho > 0.98$.

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **ITIP**, follows a three-stage pipeline:
1.  **Item Profiling (IRT):** Analyze historical performance data of $N$ models on a large benchmark using a 2-Parameter Logistic (2PL) Item Response Theory model. For each item $i$, calculate its difficulty ($\beta_i$) and discrimination ($\alpha_i$). 
2.  **Redundancy Filtering:** Construct a similarity matrix between items based on model error correlations. Use a greedy sub-modular optimization approach to select items that maximize the "Information Gain" while penalizing the selection of items that are highly correlated (i.e., redundant).
3.  **Dynamic Weighting:** Assign weights to the selected subset based on their representative power of the discarded items, ensuring the final score remains on the same scale as the original benchmark.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Primary Source:** The **MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding)** dataset, specifically the "test" splits across all 57 subjects.
*   **Alternative:** **Chatbot Arena (LMSYS)** crowd-sourced battle data (using Elo ratings as the ground truth to see if a subset of prompts can predict global Elo).
*   **Model Pool:** Performance logs from at least 30 diverse models (e.g., Llama-3, GPT-4, Mistral, Qwen) to ensure the IRT parameters are robust.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Rank Fidelity:** Spearman’s $\rho$ and Kendall’s $\tau$ between the pruned leaderboard and the full-dataset leaderboard.
*   **Efficiency Gain:** The ratio of (Original Item Count / Pruned Item Count).
*   **Stability:** The variance of model ranks when the pruned subset is applied to "held-out" models not used in the initial IRT profiling.
*   **Root Mean Square Error (RMSE):** The difference between predicted scores on the subset vs. actual scores on the full set.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Random Sampling:** Selecting $k$ items at random.
*   **Difficulty-Hard Sampling:** Selecting only the items with the lowest pass rates (the "hardest" questions).
*   **Category-Proportional Sampling:** Reducing items while maintaining the original percentage of subjects (e.g., 5% from Math, 5% from History).
*   **Variance-Based Selection:** Selecting items where model performance shows the highest variance.

### 8. Ablations
*   **IRT vs. Non-IRT:** Evaluating the subset without the discrimination parameter ($\alpha$).
*   **Redundancy Penalty:** Removing the sub-modular optimization step to see if "high discrimination" alone is sufficient (or if it leads to clusters of identical questions).
*   **Sample Size Sensitivity:** Testing the method with varying subset sizes (1%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%) to find the "elbow point" of the efficiency-accuracy curve.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Overfitting to Model Family:** A subset pruned based on Llama-style models might not accurately rank a new architecture (e.g., a state-space model or a heavily quantized model).
*   **Data Contamination:** If the pruned "high-value" items are leaked into training sets, the leaderboard's integrity collapses faster than a larger, more redundant one.
*   **Subject Neglect:** The optimization might favor "STEM" questions if they show higher discrimination, effectively "deleting" Humanities from the leaderboard if those questions are statistically noisier.
*   **Feasibility:** Requires access to raw per-item pass/fail data for a large number of models, which is not always publicly released by leaderboard maintainers. (Mitigation: Use Open LLM Leaderboard raw data).

question: Generate a research proposal on the evaluation of diversity in text generation.
answer_a:
Research Proposal: Evaluating Context-Appropriate Diversity in Neural Text
Generation## Title
CoDE: A Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation Framework for
Open-Ended Text Generation

Problem
Existing diversity metrics for text generation (Distinct-n, Self-BLEU,
Entropy-5, TTR) all share a fundamental flaw: they measure diversity as a single
scalar aggregated over a corpus, independent of the input context. This means:

• A model that generates the same generic response to every prompt can score
high on diversity if responses differ across prompts (high inter-prompt
diversity) while being pathologically repetitive within each response (low
intra-prompt diversity).
• A factual QA model that should produce low-variance answers is punished for
being "not diverse."
• There is no established way to distinguish appropriate diversity (multiple
valid paraphrases of the same meaning) from inappropriate diversity
(hallucinated facts or topic drift).

The central gap is that diversity is not a single target to maximize—it is a
distributional property that should match the conditional distribution implied
by the input.

Hypothesis
Diversity in text generation can be decomposed into two orthogonal
components—intra-response diversity (variety within a single generated text) and
inter-response diversity (variety across generations for the same input, i.e.,
model stochasticity)—and each has a context-dependent expected range that can be
estimated from the training data or human references. A model whose diversity
falls outside this expected range (too high or too low) is exhibiting a failure
mode that existing aggregate metrics miss.

Method
CoDE (Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation) proceeds in three stages:

1 Reference-conditional diversity calibration. For each input context in the
evaluation set, collect a set of human-written references (≥5 per context).
Compute per-context diversity statistics on the references to establish an
expected diversity interval per context and per diversity facet. Facets
include:

• Lexical diversity: Distinct-1, Distinct-2, corrected TTR (Herdan's TTR)
• Structural diversity: syntactic tree depth variance, POS tag entropy -
Semantic diversity: pairwise sentence-BERT cosine variance among candidate
generations for the same prompt2. Within-vs-across response decomposition.
For each model under evaluation, generate K responses per prompt (K ≥10).
Compute:
• Intra-response diversity: averaged per-response metrics (e.g., average
Self-BLEU of a response against itself in sliding windows)
• Inter-response diversity: diversity across the K generations for the same
prompt (e.g., pairwise BERTScore variance, corpus-level Distinct-n across
generations)

3 Deviation scoring. For each (model, prompt, facet) triple, measure the signed
deviation of the model's diversity from the human-established interval:

• Deviation ∈ [−1, +1] where negative = under-diverse (more repetitive than
humans), positive = over-diverse (more varied than humans, potentially
hallucinatory)
• Aggregate: mean absolute deviation across facets = CoDE score (lower is
better)

Dataset / Benchmark
Construct a multi-domain diversity benchmark spanning
contexts with intrinsically different diversity expectations:

Domain                    Expected diversity        Rationale
Factoid QA (SQuAD2.0,     Low inter + low intra     One correct answer, short
TriviaQA)
Story generation          High intra, moderate      One narrative, varied
(WritingPrompts,          inter                     style
ROCStories)
Data-to-text (WebNLG,     Low intra, moderate       Fixed facts, varied
E2E NLG)                  inter                     surface form
Open-ended dialogue       High intra + high inter   Many valid turns
(PersonaChat,
DailyDialog)
Creative continuation     High intra + high inter   Many valid completions
(Story Cloze, CommonGen)

Sample500 prompts per domain (2,500 total) with ≥5 human references each.

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary metric: CoDE score (mean absolute deviation from
the human diversity interval across all facets and domains).

2 Secondary metrics: Breakdown by facet (lexical, structural, semantic) and by
domain.
3 Validation metric: Correlation with human judgment of "appropriate diversity"
(Likert1–5) on a held-out set of200 (model, prompt, response) triples rated
by ≥3 annotators. Target: Spearman ρ ≥0.6 against the CoDE score.

Baselines| Baseline | What it measures | Expected limitation |

|---|---|---| | Distinct-1 / Distinct-2 | Surface n-gram novelty | No context
conditioning, length-biased | | Self-BLEU | Intra-corpus n-gram overlap | Single
scalar, no per-context or per-facet breakdown | | Entropy-5 / Entropy-n | n-gram
distribution uniformity | Ignores semantic and structural diversity | | Zipf
coefficient | Frequency-rank distribution fit | Only describes the tail;
insensitive to local repetition | | vMeasure (Hashimoto et al.,2019) |
Cluster-conditional diversity | Requires latent cluster assignments; not
natively context-conditional | | MAUVE (Pillutla et al.,2021) | Divergence
between model and human output distributions | Measures distribution matching,
not per-response diversity |

Ablations1. Reference-count ablation: Vary the number of human references per
prompt from1 to20. Hypothesis: the CoDE score stabilizes at ≥5 references.

2 Facet ablation: Remove each facet one at a time and measure correlation drop
with human judgment. Identifies which facet contributes most signal.
3 Pooling ablation: Replace per-prompt intervals with corpus-level intervals
(the current default in the field). Hypothesis: the per-prompt decomposition
is the main source of improvement.
4 Generation count ablation: Vary K (number of generations per prompt) from2
to50. Identifies the minimum K for stable inter-response estimates.
5 Metric-level baselines: Replace the deviation formulation with a simple
average of existing metrics conditioned on nothing. Measures the marginal
gain of context-conditional calibration.

Expected Failure Modes1. Reference quality collapse. If human references are
themselves low-quality or inconsistently diverse (e.g., crowd workers producing
minimal-effort responses), the "expected interval" becomes meaningless.
Mitigation: filter references via an automatic quality check (e.g., minimum
length, minimum Distinct-1 >0) and exclude outlying prompts where
inter-reference variance is >2σ from the domain mean.

2 Metric saturation on long-form generation. For very long generations (stories
>500 tokens), intra-response lexical diversity may saturate (all models
approach the same high Distinct-n), making the lexical facet uninformative.
Mitigation: use sliding-window diversity (window =100 tokens) and report the
minimum window diversity, not the aggregate, to capture local repetition that
longer texts hide.
3 Semantic diversity metric conflates quality with diversity. Sentence-BERT
variance could be high simply because generations are incoherent rather than
genuinely diverse. Mitigation: compute semantic diversity only over
generations that pass a minimum fluency/coherence threshold (e.g., perplexity
< a domain-specific cutoff). Flag the model's quality-diversity trade-off
explicitly as a secondary diagnostic.
4 Domain boundary ambiguity. The "expected diversity" for an ambiguous prompt
(e.g., a news headline that could be either factual or editorial) may not
fall cleanly into one domain bin. Mitigation: report per-prompt deviations
rather than only domain aggregates, and provide prompt-level visualization
for outlier analysis.
5 Inter-response diversity is confounded by sampling temperature. A model run
at temperature1.0 will naturally produce more inter-response variation than
at temperature0.1. The CoDE score must hold sampling hyperparameters fixed
across all models, or the benchmark becomes a comparison of sampling
strategies rather than model architectures. Mitigation: standardize to
temperature =0.7, top-p =0.9 for all models, and include a sensitivity
experiment reporting how CoDE changes with temperature.
